title: DON’T MARRY SOMEONE JUST TO MAKE SOMEONE ELSE JEALOUS, ANGRY, OR IMPRESSED
paragraphs: DON’T MARRY SOMEONE JUST TO MAKE SOMEONE ELSE JEALOUS, ANGRY, OR IMPRESSED
Because the person standing beside you at the altar should never become collateral damage in a war they didn’t start.
There is something heartbreaking about saying “I do” while secretly hoping somebody else hears about it.
Read that again.
Because sometimes a wedding is not really about love.
Sometimes it is revenge wearing white.
Sometimes it is insecurity carrying flowers.
Sometimes it is loneliness dressed beautifully enough that nobody notices it is still loneliness.
Sometimes it is a wounded person quietly saying, “Look at me now.”
And sometimes the person smiling beside them has absolutely no idea that they have just been recruited into somebody else’s unfinished emotional war.
You wanted your ex to regret losing you.
You wanted the person who rejected you to finally see your worth.
You wanted your parents to stop questioning you.
You wanted your friends to believe you were happy.
You wanted people online to see the photographs, the ring, the celebration, the honeymoon, the captions.
Anything.
Jealousy.
Regret.
Pain.
Loss.
And somewhere underneath all of it was a wounded voice whispering:
“Now they’ll know what they lost.”
But what happens when the person you married eventually realizes they were never the destination?
They were the message.
That is where this gets serious.
Because marriage is far too sacred to turn another human being into your evidence that you have moved on.
Jesus said something about marriage that should make us tremble before treating it casually:
“Therefore what God has joined together, let no one separate.”
Matthew 19:6
The Greek behind “joined together” is συνέζευξεν — synezeuxen, from a verb carrying the sense of joining or yoking together.
Jesus was not describing marriage as an Instagram announcement.
He was speaking about a union.
A covenantal joining.
Two lives being bound together before God.

And if you are thinking about marriage because you need somebody else to become jealous, angry, impressed, or sorry, you need to hear this before rings are purchased, invitations are mailed, and promises are spoken:
Another person’s heart is not a weapon.
Their future is not your revenge.
Their affection is not medicine for your wounded ego.
And marriage is not a stage where you prove to your past that you won.
Because eventually the wedding ends.
The photographs stop trending.
The congratulations slow down.
The flowers die.
The dress gets stored away.
Everybody goes home.
And then there are two people standing inside ordinary life together.
Bills.
Fatigue.
Misunderstandings.
Family problems.
Sickness.
Temptation.
Disappointment.
Sex.
Forgiveness.
Laundry.
Prayer.
Children, perhaps.
Loss.
Growing older.
Monday mornings when nobody is applauding.
That is marriage too.
And the person you marry deserves someone who chose them when there was no audience watching.
They deserve to know:
“I would still choose you if my ex never found out.”
“I would still choose you if nobody envied us.”
“I would still choose you if our wedding received five likes instead of five thousand.”
“I would still choose you if nobody was impressed.”
“I would still choose you because I am not using you to communicate with somebody from my past.”
That kind of honesty matters because Scripture does not define love by the reaction it produces in spectators.
It describes love by what it gives to the beloved.
Paul writes:
1 Corinthians 13:4
The Greek word translated “love” is ἀγάπη — agapē.
And then comes a devastating contrast for anyone using romance to provoke jealousy:
οὐ ζηλοῖ — ou zēloi
Love “does not envy” or is not consumed by jealousy.
Then:
οὐ περπερεύεται — ou perpereuetai
Love does not boast.
Think about that.
If the driving energy behind your relationship is, “Wait until they see us,” Scripture is asking you to examine what is actually happening inside your heart.
Not because posting wedding photographs is wrong.
Not because celebrating your spouse publicly is wrong.
Not because being happy after heartbreak is wrong.
But because there is an enormous difference between celebrating someone you love and using someone you claim to love as a billboard aimed at somebody else.
One says:
“I am grateful for you.”
The other secretly says:
“I hope they see you.”
Those are not the same heart.
And God sees the difference even when Facebook does not.
Maybe that hurts.
Maybe while reading this, somebody immediately came into your mind.
Maybe you are already dating someone good, but if you were brutally honest before God, part of what attracted you to the relationship was how it would make someone else feel.
Maybe you keep imagining your ex seeing the engagement announcement.
Maybe you are moving faster than wisdom allows because being married feels like proof that you were desirable after all.
Maybe somebody humiliated you.
Cheated on you.
Abandoned you.
Replaced you.
Ghosted you.
Told you nobody would ever want you.
Maybe they married someone else.
And now there is a part of you that desperately wants your own spectacular ending.
That wound is real.
But please hear this:
You do not have to destroy another person's future to prove that somebody else failed to recognize your value.
You do not need a spouse to become evidence that you were worth loving.
Your deepest worth was never supposed to come from whether another wounded human being chose you.
For the Christian, identity reaches somewhere much deeper.
It reaches the cross.
“But God demonstrates his own love for us in this: While we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
Romans 5:8
Before your wedding.
Before your relationship status.
Before somebody finally recognized your beauty.
Before anybody regretted losing you.
Before you managed to make your life look impressive.
Christ loved sinners.
That changes the question.
Instead of asking:
“How can I prove they were wrong about me?”
The Gospel asks:
“What if I no longer need their regret to become free?”
That is a completely different kind of healing.
Because revenge keeps you emotionally connected to the person you claim you have moved beyond.
You are still arranging your life around their eyes.
Still wondering what they think.
Still measuring whether they noticed.
Still hoping they hurt.
Still waiting for their reaction.
They may not even know they still occupy that much space inside you.
But Jesus does.
And He does not expose wounds merely to shame wounded people.
He calls sinners into the light because grace does its deepest work where pretending finally ends.
Maybe the most spiritual thing you can do before marrying someone is not choose flowers.
Not choose a venue.
Not choose a photographer.
Maybe it is getting alone with God and asking:
“Jesus, why do I really want this?”
And then staying quiet long enough to hear an answer you might not like.
Scripture says:
“Search me, God, and know my heart; test me and know my anxious thoughts.”
Psalm 139:23
The Hebrew begins:
חָקְרֵנִי אֵל וְדַע לְבָבִי
ḥoqreni El, veda levavi.
“Search me, God, and know my heart.”
That is a dangerous prayer when you have become skilled at explaining your motives to yourself.
Search me.
Not my ex.
Not the person who hurt me.
Not my parents.
Not everybody judging my relationship.
Me.
Lord, search me.
Show me whether I am choosing covenant or chasing validation.
Show me whether I love this person or merely love what being with this person says about me.
Show me whether I am preparing for marriage or staging a comeback.
Show me whether I want a spouse or an audience.
Show me whether I am healed enough to love someone without secretly asking them to pay a debt somebody else created.
That prayer can save years of pain.
Because marriage magnifies what dating can sometimes hide.
Unhealed comparison eventually appears.
Unresolved attachment eventually speaks.
Resentment leaks.
Pride leaks.
Fear leaks.
And eventually the innocent person beside you begins asking the question nobody should have to ask inside a marriage:
“Are you actually here with me?”
Imagine hearing that from your husband.
Imagine hearing it from your wife.
Imagine discovering that every romantic photograph had a ghost standing just outside the frame.
Someone from the past.
Someone your spouse was still trying to impress.
Someone they were still trying to punish.
Someone whose opinion somehow remained more powerful than your presence.
That is why this is not merely relationship advice.
This is about loving your neighbor truthfully.
It is about refusing to use another image-bearer of God as emotional ammunition.
It is about repentance.
And repentance is not simply feeling terrible about yourself.
The New Testament word often translated “repent” is μετανοέω — metanoeō, carrying the idea of changing one’s mind or turning in response to truth.
Jesus begins His public proclamation with:
“Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has come near.”
Matthew 4:17
Repentance says:
“I cannot keep walking this direction just because my wound explains why I started walking it.”
Your pain may explain your temptation.
It does not have to become your master.
And perhaps that is exactly where somebody reading this is standing.
You have not married them yet.
Good.
There is still time to become honest.
Do not panic.
Do not immediately destroy a healthy relationship simply because you recognize mixed motives inside yourself.
Human motives can be complicated.
Bring them into the light.
Slow down if necessary.
Seek wise, biblically grounded counsel.
Talk honestly with mature believers who are not impressed by appearances.
And if the relationship is moving toward marriage, premarital counseling with a trustworthy pastor or qualified Christian counselor can uncover things romantic chemistry often cannot.
But whatever you do, stop asking another human being to heal something only Christ can ultimately reach.
Your future husband cannot become your Savior.
Your future wife cannot become your Savior.
Marriage cannot become your resurrection.
Being desired cannot become your justification.
A wedding cannot wash away shame.
A ring cannot crucify your past.
Jesus can meet you there.
Jesus can forgive.
Jesus can restore.
Jesus can teach wounded people how to love without turning love into retaliation.
This is why the Gospel is so much bigger than “find the right person.”
The Gospel tells us that our deepest problem is not singleness.
It is sin.
And our deepest answer is not marriage.
It is Christ.
Paul writes:
Ephesians 1:7
The word translated “redemption” is ἀπολύτρωσις — apolytrōsis.
Redemption.
Release purchased at a cost.
That is what Jesus offers.
Not cosmetic healing.
Not a carefully curated life designed to make the people who rejected you jealous.
Freedom.
You can become so free in Christ that you no longer need the person who hurt you to suffer before you can have peace.
So free that you can stop checking whether they viewed your story.
So free that you do not need to manufacture happiness where they can see it.
So free that your future marriage does not have to become a courtroom where you finally prove your worth.
So free that when you eventually stand beside somebody and say, “I do,” you can actually mean:
“I am here with you.”
Not them.
You.
And if you already married for some of the wrong reasons?
Then perhaps this article became uncomfortable several paragraphs ago.
Maybe you recognized yourself and felt your stomach tighten.
Do not use conviction as permission to abandon covenant casually.
The same Christ who exposes sin also calls us toward confession, forgiveness, faithfulness, truth, and transformation.
Your beginning may have been messy.
Your motives may have been mixed.
Your marriage may carry scars from decisions you now regret.
But the Gospel Warrior message exists for precisely this kind of human story:
Because Jesus Rewrites Everything.
Not because Jesus pretends the earlier chapters never happened.
He redeems people inside stories that really happened.
Peter really denied Him.
Paul really persecuted Christians.
The Samaritan woman really had a complicated relational history.
The thief really hung on a cross because he was guilty.
Christian grace is not God announcing that sin never mattered.
Grace is astonishing precisely because sin mattered enough for Christ to go to the cross.
And resurrection tells us failure does not have to write the final sentence.
Maybe your marriage began partly out of jealousy.
Then repent of jealousy.
Maybe it began from pride.
Repent of pride.
Maybe you used your spouse.
Confess where wisdom permits and seek help in repairing what your selfishness damaged.
Then start learning how to choose them now.
Love them now.
Honor them now.
Pray for them now.
Become faithful now.
You cannot rewrite yesterday.
But surrendered to Christ, you do not have to keep repeating yesterday tomorrow.
And if you are single right now, please do not become so desperate to prove that you are lovable that you accept a covenant you are not ready to honor.
Being unmarried is not humiliation.
Being rejected is not proof that God rejected you.
Watching somebody else get married first does not mean heaven forgot your address.
And somebody else's relationship is not God's deadline for yours.
Wait with wisdom.
Heal honestly.
Grow in Christ.
Learn contentment that does not depend upon romantic attention.
Become the kind of person capable of loving another person rather than consuming them.
Then, if God leads you into marriage, enter it understanding that biblical marriage is not primarily a trophy for two attractive people who finally found happiness.
Paul ultimately points Christian marriage toward something astonishing:
“Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her.”
Ephesians 5:25
Look at the direction of that love.
Christ gave Himself.
Marriage shaped by Christ therefore moves away from:
“What can this person prove about me?”
toward:
“How can I faithfully love this person before God?”
That is where jealousy begins losing oxygen.
That is where pride starts dying.
That is where performance becomes covenant.
That is where the ex finally disappears from the room.
And perhaps that is the sentence somebody desperately needed tonight:
The ex needs to disappear from the room.
Not physically.
Emotionally.
Stop letting someone who left become an invisible third person inside the relationship God may be asking you to steward faithfully.
Stop dressing for their reaction.
Stop posting for their reaction.
Stop dating for their reaction.
Stop marrying for their reaction.
Stop building your future around somebody who belongs to your past.
Bring the wound to Jesus.
Tell Him the ugly truth.
“Lord, I wanted them jealous.”
“Lord, I wanted them sorry.”
“Lord, I wanted everybody impressed.”
“Lord, I wanted to prove something.”
“Lord, I am still angry.”
“Lord, I am not as healed as I pretend.”
That prayer may not look impressive enough for social media.
But heaven has never required your performance.
Christ calls you into truth.
And maybe tonight truth sounds like tears.
Maybe truth sounds like repentance.
Maybe truth sounds like finally admitting that you have been calling revenge “moving on.”
If this exposed something hidden, do not hide behind embarrassment.
Not because typing words saves anyone.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes bringing what has lived silently in darkness into honest Christian community is where pretending begins to lose its grip.
And somebody reading your comment may realize they are not the only believer fighting this battle.

Not because every sentence will feel comfortable tomorrow, but because there may come a night when loneliness starts negotiating with your convictions and you need to remember why marriage should never become revenge.
But before you leave this page, remember the person whose face appeared in your mind when you first read the title.
Maybe it was your ex.
Maybe it was the person you are dating.
Maybe it was yourself.
Now imagine standing at an altar someday.
Someone is looking into your eyes.
They are trusting you with years they can never get back.
They are trusting you with mornings and midnight conversations, weakness and aging, intimacy and disappointment, sickness and celebration.
They are trusting you with a heart God never gave you permission to use as ammunition.
When you look back into their eyes, may there be nobody else in the room you are secretly trying to impress.
No ghost.
No rival.
No revenge.
No audience.
Just truth.
Just covenant.
Just two imperfect people desperately dependent upon a perfect Savior.
Because the greatest victory after somebody breaks your heart is not making them jealous.
It is becoming so surrendered to Jesus that you no longer need them to be jealous at all.
Do not use somebody's heart to send a message to your past—place your wounded heart in the hands of Christ, and let Him write a future that no longer needs revenge to feel redeemed.
